"Scuttle" is a fascinating verb because it has three distinct meanings that are quite different from one another. Mastering all three is what makes you truly understand this word.
Meaning 1: To move quickly with short, hurried steps

This is the most physically visual meaning. When a person or animal scuttles, they move fast but in a slightly awkward, rushed, or furtive (sneaky) way — think of the quick, busy scurrying of a crab, a mouse, or a cockroach.

It's not elegant running. It carries a sense of someone moving hastily, often to avoid being seen or because they are in a mild panic.

Examples:

  • The mouse scuttled across the kitchen floor and disappeared behind the refrigerator.
  • When the boss walked in unexpectedly, the employee scuttled back to his desk.
  • Crabs scuttle sideways along the beach.

The feeling it conveys: busyness, slight nervousness, haste, and a lack of grace. If someone "strolls," they are relaxed. If they "scuttle," they are hurrying in a fidgety, almost scrambling way.
Meaning 2: To deliberately sink a ship

This meaning is very specific and powerful. To scuttle a ship means to intentionally sink it by making holes in its hull (its body), opening water valves, or flooding its compartments from within.

The absolute key word here is deliberately. A ship that sinks because of a storm or an accident has not been scuttled. Scuttling is always a conscious, planned act.

Why would anyone sink their own ship?

This is a great question, and understanding the reasons helps the word stick:

  • To prevent the enemy from capturing it — During war, if a crew knew their ship was about to be seized by the enemy, they would rather destroy it themselves than let the enemy use it. This is an act of denial.
  • To block a harbour or channel — A sunken ship becomes an obstacle. Armies have scuttled ships in narrow waterways to stop enemy vessels from passing through.
  • For insurance fraud — Unscrupulous ship owners have scuttled their own vessels to falsely claim insurance money.
  • To create an artificial reef — Old ships are sometimes deliberately sunk to create underwater habitats for marine life.

Examples:

  • The captain ordered the crew to scuttle the warship before the enemy could board it.
  • The vessel was scuttled in shallow water to form an artificial reef for divers.
Meaning 3: To deliberately ruin or kill a plan, deal, or effort

This is the figurative (metaphorical) meaning, and it is extremely common in modern English — probably the meaning you will encounter most often in newspapers, politics, and business.

When you scuttle a plan, a deal, a negotiation, or a project, you deliberately destroy it, wreck it, or cause it to fail — often secretly or from the inside.

Just like scuttling a ship (sinking it on purpose), scuttling a plan means intentionally bringing it down. The destruction is not accidental.

Examples:

  • The senator's last-minute opposition scuttled the peace deal that had taken years to negotiate.
  • A leaked memo scuttled the company's plans to merge with its rival.
  • He scuttled his own chances of promotion by arriving late to the most important meeting of the year.
  • The new government scuttled several infrastructure projects that the previous government had started.

The crucial nuance: Something can only be scuttled if it was going reasonably well or had a real chance of succeeding. You scuttle something that is afloat — just like a ship. The word implies that without the deliberate interference, the plan would have survived.
How to Tell the Three Meanings Apart in Context

The context almost always makes it crystal clear:

  • If the subject is a living creature moving around → Meaning 1 (hurried movement).
  • If the object of the verb is a ship or vessel → Meaning 2 (sinking it).
  • If the object is a plan, deal, bill, agreement, effort, or project → Meaning 3 (destroying it deliberately).
The One Thread That Connects All Three Meanings

Even though the three meanings seem very different, they all share a common emotional quality: urgency and deliberateness.

  • The animal scuttling is moving with purposeful urgency.
  • The crew scuttling a ship is taking a drastic, deliberate action.
  • The politician scuttling a bill is making a decisive, intentional move to destroy it.

In all three cases, there is agency — someone or something is doing something on purpose, not drifting or acting by accident. That quality of intentional, decisive action is the soul of this word.
